source.title: Pruning for Interpretable, Feature-Preserving Circuits in CNNs
source.authors: Christopher J. Hamblin; Talia Konkle; G. Alvarez

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a feature with apparently disparate image categories is produced by one shared computation or by distinct image-specific computations, using category-conditioned circuit pruning rather than the original visual-inspection method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports category-specific subcircuit results for polysemantic Alexnet filters. General circuit-preservation results and the circle-detector analysis do not bear on these claim versions. Clustering settings and values used to select features are not separate outcome rows.
record.test_reason: Uses category-conditioned subcircuit pruning in Alexnet to ask whether a polysemantic filter's responses to two unrelated categories come from one shared hidden feature or from separate computations. The authors frame this explicitly as the shared-feature hypothesis versus distinct features. This bears on V6, and on V1 through the identified filters.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that polysemantic filters can be split into category-specific subcircuits. This favors distinct entangled features over a hidden shared feature for Conv5:9, and they say it holds for Conv5:161 and 'many such features'. Subcircuits share layer-1 kernels but diverge later.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces saliency-based pruning of convolutional kernels to extract feature-preserving and image-specific subcircuits, rather than the original source's visual inspection of circuits and features.
record.method_sensitivity: The subcircuit result depends on the target image group: semantic category-specific targets yield divergent circuits, while random halves of the same mixed groups yield overlapping results. The reported Conv5:9 subcircuits share layer 1 computations but diverge in subsequent layers.
record.problems: The polysemanticity evidence is based on selected Alexnet filters and qualitative category descriptions. The subcircuit curves and Conv5:9 IoU are not reported numerically in the text, and the paper does not quantify how prevalent the phenomenon is across models or features.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for the circle-detector and general circuit-preservation experiments: they do not measure polysemanticity or the claim versions tested here.

untested.parts: InceptionV1 and standard (unregularized) models; how common polysemantic filters are. Only two hand-picked filters are reported, and the screen is said to find 'many' without a count.
How often canonical polysemantic neurons hide a shared feature in general; any neurons beyond Conv5:9 and Conv5:161 in regularized Alexnet.
Superposition or compression is cited as one possible account (Elhage et al.), but capacity pressure is not tested.
Not tested. Only one regularized Alexnet is used for polysemanticity, with no comparison of rates.

missing.what: Category-specific subcircuit outcome for Conv5:161 (whether the monkey and text subcircuits preserve the other category, and their IoU). Stated only as the split 'works'; values are in the figure only.

The clustering screen's statement that it identifies 'many' filters with intuitive polysemanticity, and that it rarely returned more than 2 clusters (Figure 12 examples). No count of polysemantic filters is given.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is qualitative: curves and IoU are in figures only, with no numbers or uncertainty. Candidate filters were chosen because their top-activating patches form separate clusters in the layer's representation space. That makes some separability of the subcircuits plausible by construction, which weakens the V6 challenge somewhat. All polysemanticity analyses use a sparsity-regularized Alexnet fine-tuned to 53% top-1 accuracy. Circle-detector and general circuit-preservation results do not bear on the claim versions.

versions.untested_parts: Tests examples in Alexnet, not InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55; does not quantify how common such mixed responses are across neurons or models.
No transformer language models or language inputs.
Discusses compression as a possible account, but does not test feature-to-neuron capacity pressure or superposition.
Does not test initialization, regularization or training noise as causes of polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient.
Does not compare polysemanticity rates across activation functions, architectures or regularization, nor test a performance-cost tradeoff for reducing it.
Tests category-specific subcircuits in selected Alexnet filters, not how often canonical polysemantic neurons generally have a shared job.
Does not compare activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods as measures of polysemanticity.

rows.value: The patches are described as belonging to terrier faces and metal cylinders with horizontal lines.
rows.note: The paper describes these as distinct categories and uses this filter for the category-specific subcircuit analysis.

relation.reason: The study's own subcircuit results bear directly on the shared-feature question in V6, and its filters are instances for V1.

tranche.reason: A different method (saliency-based subcircuit pruning) aimed explicitly at whether a polysemantic filter detects one shared feature or several distinct ones.

source_check.notes: Both filters come from an HDBScan clustering screen on the sparsity-regularized AlexNet (53.03% vs 56.55% top-1). All subcircuit results are qualitative curve and IoU readings with no numbers in the text. The paper hedges the layer-1 sharing ('It seems'); 'share only in layer 1' means the subcircuits deviate later, not that later IoU is zero. Elhage et al. is cited for the entanglement view, but V3 is not tested.

statements.correction: Text: regularized AlexNet Conv5:9 = terrier faces and metal cylinders (Sec 6.1); conv5:161 = monkey faces and written text (App 8.10); candidates found by an HDBScan screen of the top-300 activations (App 8.9). Code y, random-split control y, regularized model 53.03% vs original 56.55% top-1; no count of polysemantic filters given.

Conv5:9: each category subcircuit's activations for the other category deviate at lower sparsities than its own target. Layer 1 computations are shared, and the subcircuits deviate in later layers (no IoU numbers given). Random 50/50 split: curves overlap and IoU is high (control). Conv5:161: the appendix says the same analysis works (Fig 13) but gives no numbers.
Category-based targets give separable subcircuits. Random 50/50 halves of the terrier and metal patches do not (curves overlap, high IoU across layers). No numbers given.
